title: Same-Unit Comparer
context: Grade 5, the pages on comparing different measures. An adult sees a comparison of two numbers. What the pages are doing is refusing to compare until both measures are in the same unit, because the bigger number is not always the bigger measure.

writeup.why: Compare measures by writing them in the same unit first, tell when two are equal, find by how much one is more, and put several in ascending or descending order.
writeup.look: Measure cards along the top, and below them bars standing against one scale once the cards share a unit.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Same-Unit Comparer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of measures put in the same unit. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The measure cards lie in a row across the top of the area at y 230, each 220 by 90, in deep blue, labelled Given, each in the form the question wrote it. The Same unit button stands at x 900, y 230, with a violet Unit fact beside it that names the link between the two units. Pressed, it rewrites each card in the smaller unit of the pair and stands each up as a bar rising from one baseline along y 700, the bars 120 wide and drawn to one scale, the rewritten measures green, labelled Same measure, above each bar. The sign slot sits between two bars at y 450 and takes less than, greater than or equals. On the third phase the Take away button stands at x 900, y 330, and pressed it lays the shorter bar over the longer, the covered part rose, labelled Taken away, and the part that sticks out green, labelled Answer, with its unit. On the fourth phase a shelf runs along y 700 from x 120 to x 1060, and the bar being dragged is amber. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a delete key, and a key for each unit of the pair. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last bars stay on the shelf in order, with their cards above them in the same unit.

phases.win: the sign clicks between the two bars, and the taller bar's card turns green
phases.does: presses Same unit, reads both bars, and sets the sign between them
phases.goal: write both measures in the same unit, then compare the numbers
phases.says: Same unit first. Which bar stands taller?
phases.check: Away from the screen: which is longer, your pencil or your ruler, and did you measure them in the same unit?
phases.feels: two bars rising from one baseline and one plainly standing taller
phases.hands: Weigh two bags of beans on a kitchen scale, write one weight in kilograms and grams and the other in grams, then write both in grams before saying which is heavier.
phases.tries: First rung: rewrite only the mixed card in the smaller unit. Second rung: compare two numbers now in one unit. Third rung: the same task on two lengths, before the question's own weights return.

wrong.why: a bigger number usually means more, so the card with more digits feels heavier
wrong.move: sets the greater than sign before pressing Same unit, choosing the card with the bigger-looking number
wrong.screen: the sign stays where the child set it, and the bars stand up beside it so the child sees which is taller, with the Same unit button lit amber

wrong.why: the larger unit feels like it decides everything
wrong.move: compares only the kilograms part of the mixed measure with the other card
wrong.screen: the grams part of the mixed card is lit amber, and its bar grows by that part in steps while the child's sign stays

phases.screen: two cards, one a mixed measure and one in grams, and the Same unit button
phases.soWhat: write both measures in the same unit, then compare the numbers

phases.does: presses Same unit and sees the two bars stand level, then sets the equals sign
phases.goal: two measures in different forms are equal when they are the same in the same unit
phases.check: Away from the screen: say one length two ways, once in metres and centimetres and once in centimetres.
phases.feels: two different-looking cards standing exactly level
phases.hands: Write one length in metres and centimetres on one card and in centimetres on another. Lay two strips of paper cut to each and see that they match.
phases.tries: First rung: rewrite the mixed card in centimetres. Second rung: compare it with the other card. Third rung: the same task with a whole number of metres, before the question's own cards return.

wrong.why: different-looking numbers seem like they must be different lengths
wrong.move: sets less than because the two cards look different
wrong.screen: the sign stays, and the two bars stand up beside it exactly level, with the equals sign lit amber in the tray

wrong.why: writing the digits side by side feels like changing the unit
wrong.move: picks the option whose digits follow the mixed measure's digits in order
wrong.screen: the chosen card stands up as a bar beside the mixed measure's bar, the two tops seen apart, and the chosen card is lit amber

phases.screen: two cards, a mixed measure and the same length in centimetres
phases.soWhat: two measures in different forms are equal when they are the same in the same unit

phases.win: the rose part is covered, and the part that sticks out turns green with its unit
phases.does: puts both in the same unit, presses Take away, and types the difference with its unit
phases.goal: to find by how much, take the smaller from the larger in the same unit
phases.says: Lay the shorter one over. How much sticks out?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two ribbons, one longer. How would you find how much longer, without a sum?
phases.feels: the shorter bar sliding over the longer and the leftover part lighting up

wrong.why: the numbers are there, and taking away seems ready to go
wrong.move: presses Take away while the two cards are still in different units
wrong.screen: the two bars cannot be laid over each other and stand apart, each with its own unit lit amber, until Same unit is pressed

wrong.why: the number feels like the whole answer once the taking away is done
wrong.move: types the difference without its unit
wrong.screen: the difference waits in the slot uncoloured, and the unit keys on the pad are lit amber

phases.screen: two capacity cards and the Take away button
phases.soWhat: to find by how much, take the smaller from the larger in the same unit

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the last bar drops into place, the four bars rise along the shelf like steps, and a small ball rolls up them from the shortest to the tallest.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet compared. On the first phase two cards lie across the top, one a mixed measure and one in grams, with the Same unit button beside them. On the second two cards lie there, a mixed measure and a length in centimetres. On the third two capacity cards lie there with the Take away button waiting. On the fourth four weight cards in mixed forms lie above an empty shelf. One thing moves, once: the Same unit button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any measures typed onto the cards, put in one unit, compared, taken away and ordered. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on comparing, equal measures, differences and order.
voiceLines: Some measure cards, each written its own way.
Same unit first. Which bar stands taller?
Lay the shorter one over. How much sticks out?
Same unit first. Now smallest to largest.
Free play. Lay out any cards and stand them up side by side.
Are they in the same unit yet? Press Same unit and look again.
You put every measure in one unit before you compared.

observations.why: the number alone says nothing until the two measures are in the same unit.
observations.soWhat: put both measures in the same unit first, then compare the numbers.
observations.observe: A card with a bigger number stood as the shorter bar.

observations.why: they are one measure written in two forms.
observations.soWhat: equal measures can look different, and the same unit shows it.
observations.observe: Two cards that looked quite different stood exactly level.

observations.why: by how much means the larger take away the smaller, in one unit.
observations.soWhat: a difference is a measure too, and it keeps its unit.
observations.observe: Only the part that stuck out past the shorter bar was the difference.

observations.why: in one unit, a bigger number is a bigger measure.
observations.soWhat: ordering is comparing, done a few times over.
observations.observe: Once the bars were up, putting them in order was just reading their heights.

source_tool.description: Measure cards lie across the top of the working area, each written in its own form, some mixed and some in one unit, in deep blue, labelled Given. A Same unit button rewrites every card in the smaller unit of the pair and stands each up as a bar against one scale along the bottom of the area, the rewritten measures in green, labelled Same measure, with a violet unit fact beside the button, such as 1 kg = 1000 g. A sign slot between two bars takes less than, greater than or equals. On the third phase a Take away button lays the shorter bar over the longer, the covered part rose, labelled Taken away, and what sticks out is the difference, green, labelled Answer, with its unit. On the fourth phase four bars can be dragged along a shelf into ascending or descending order, and the bar being moved is amber. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the measures put in the same unit.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Are they in the same unit yet? Press Same unit and look again.
voice.opening: Some measure cards, each written its own way.
voice.onFinish: You put every measure in one unit before you compared.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Lay out any cards and stand them up side by side.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has guessed which of three bottles holds the most, poured each into a measuring jug, and written the capacities in millilitres. The tool is what stands the measures up side by side in one unit, which the list on paper cannot.

answer_key.rule: Write every measure in the same unit before comparing. Then compare the numbers: the larger number in the same unit is the larger measure. Two measures are equal when they are the same in the same unit. To find by how much, take the smaller from the larger in the same unit. Ascending order goes from smallest to largest, and descending order from largest to smallest.
answer_key.wrong: A sign or an order set before Same unit is pressed stays where the child put it, and the bars then stand up beside it so the child sees which is longer. A difference taken in two different units is shown as two bars that cannot be laid over each other until they share a unit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: First write both in the same unit, grams.
3 kg is 3000 g, so 3 kg 90 g is 3090 g.
items.question: Which is heavier, 3 kg 90 g or 3150 g?
items.checkpoint: Write both measures in the same unit before comparing.
items.misconception: Choosing 3 kg 90 g because it has kilograms in it, without writing both in grams first.

steps: 6 m is 600 cm, so 6 m 5 cm is 605 cm.
Both are 605 cm in the same unit.
So the two lengths are equal.
items.answer: Yes. They are the same length.
items.question: Is 6 m 5 cm the same length as 605 cm?
items.checkpoint: Two measures are equal when they are the same in the same unit.
items.misconception: Reading 6 m 5 cm as sixty-five centimetres by leaving out the zero, and so calling the two lengths different.

steps: Write both in millilitres: 2 L 640 mL is 2640 mL.
Compare: 2640 > 2475, so the pot holds more.
Take the smaller from the larger: 2640 - 2475 = 165.
So the pot holds 165 mL more than the kettle.
items.question: A pot holds 2 L 640 mL and a kettle holds 2475 mL. Which holds more, and by how much?
items.checkpoint: To find by how much, take the smaller from the larger in the same unit.
items.misconception: Taking 475 from 640 and ignoring the litres, which answers a different question.

steps: Write all four in grams: 1400 g, 1040 g, 1004 g and 1410 g.
Ascending order goes from smallest to largest.
So the order is 1 kg 4 g, 1040 g, 1 kg 400 g, 1410 g.
items.question: Put these weights in ascending order: 1 kg 400 g, 1040 g, 1 kg 4 g, 1410 g.
items.checkpoint: Put every measure in the same unit, then order the numbers.
items.misconception: Ordering by the digits as they look and placing 1 kg 4 g last, because 4 g was read as the most grams.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which is longer, 3 m 20 cm or 330 cm?
items.final_answer: 330 cm, because 3 m 20 cm is 320 cm

items.question: Do 5 L 300 mL and 5300 mL hold the same amount?
A green ribbon is 1 m 85 cm long and a red ribbon is 164 cm long. How much longer is the green ribbon?
items.final_answer: 21 cm longer, because 1 m 85 cm is 185 cm and 185 - 164 = 21

items.question: Which is lighter, 4 kg 60 g or 4600 g?
items.final_answer: 4 kg 60 g, because it is 4060 g

items.question: Which of these is the same length as 3 km 50 m: 3500 m, 3050 m or 3005 m?
A sack of flour weighs 5 kg 125 g and a sack of lentils weighs 4 kg 980 g. Which is heavier, and by how much?
Put these in descending order: 3 L 75 mL, 3570 mL, 3 L 7 mL, 3705 mL.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: rewrites every card in the smaller unit and stands it up as a bar
takes less than, greater than or equals between two bars
lays the shorter bar over the longer to show the difference
moves a bar along the shelf into order
types a measure or a difference

teaching_notes: Nothing is compared until both measures are in the same unit; the smaller unit keeps every number whole. Line the numbers up in one unit and then use the signs. When a question asks by how much, take the smaller from the larger in the same unit and name the unit of the difference. Check the zeros inside a mixed measure: 1 kg 4 g is 1004 g, not 1400 g.
generation_prompt: Build a measure comparing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Measure cards in deep blue lie across the top of the working area, each in its own form. A Same unit button rewrites every card in the smaller unit, in green, and stands each up as a bar against one scale, with a violet unit fact beside the button. A sign slot between two bars takes less than, greater than or equals. A Take away button lays the shorter bar over the longer, the covered part rose and the part left green with its unit. On the last phase four bars are dragged along a shelf into order, the bar being moved amber. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Press Same unit first. Then compare the bars, find equal ones, lay one over another to see by how much, or drag them into order.
